title: What will bring high streets back to life?
label: 17 November 2026 · High streets and business rates
summary: The committee heard that rising business costs are putting pressure on retailers, pubs and other independent businesses, but witnesses disagreed over whether business rates relief reaches businesses or landlords. They argued that high streets need more than tax changes: local areas need tailored plans, stronger local leadership and the skills and resources to carry them out. A second panel debated major changes to business rates, local government funding and a proposed tax on online sales, without reaching agreement on the best approach.

chapters.title: Rising costs and pressure on businesses
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said business costs are threatening jobs and independent businesses, although they differed on which forms of support would help most.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What impact has the April 2026 business rates revaluation had on shops, pubs and other hospitality businesses?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: It’s been catastrophic for hospitality. Average rates rose by 76% for pubs and 115% for hotels. The Government’s later 20% discount for pubs, social clubs and live music venues helps, but it isn’t enough.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Retailers faced several changes at once: the revaluation, the ending of earlier reliefs, and new rates that were lower for some businesses but higher for larger properties. Taken together, retailers are paying about £1.1 billion more.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: The swings in bills make it hard to plan. Hospitality was hit particularly hard because property values had fallen at the previous revaluation and then rose sharply.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Have higher employment costs and energy bills added to the strain?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Yes. Hospitality has lost more than 100,000 jobs, mostly held by 18-to-24-year-olds. Part-time pub jobs that used to help young people get work are much harder to find.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: I support the higher minimum wage, but businesses have also faced higher rates, energy bills and national insurance. The timing has made it difficult to absorb.

turns.speaker: Lee Dillon
turns.text: You support the recommendation to reduce employers’ national insurance costs when they hire young people?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Yes. A pub employing 20 young people could save about £15,000 a year under the suggested changes. It’s a useful start, though a VAT cut would make a much bigger difference.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Retail has lost about 120,000 jobs, and its tax burden has risen 20% in two years. The national living wage should rise, but businesses have struggled with increases above inflation, especially after the national insurance rise.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Retail and hospitality are important first jobs. Lowering employers’ national insurance costs for entry-level jobs could make it easier to offer young people part-time work around their studies.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: The independent shops, cafés and bakeries give high streets their character, so they need support. I’m also concerned that large chains can arrange their affairs so they pay less corporation tax than local businesses.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Small businesses are especially worried about energy costs, rents and short leases. They often can’t afford to improve a property they don’t own, so their buildings become run-down and they have less money to attract customers.

chapters.title: Who benefits from business rates relief?
chapters.takeaway: The panel disagreed over whether rate cuts help tenants or are eventually absorbed into rents, while agreeing that unpredictability can discourage investment.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Some argue that rates relief for shops and pubs mostly ends up benefiting landlords through higher rents. If so, would other kinds of support work better?

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: I don’t accept that relief is simply swallowed by rent. Property markets don’t adjust instantly: rates are reassessed only every three years, and landlords may avoid lowering rents because it can affect their borrowing.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: If the market worked perfectly, we wouldn’t have so many empty properties. More generally, business rates are too large a part of the tax burden compared with other developed countries.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Would a more predictable system help businesses invest for the long term?

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Yes. Businesses need fewer sudden changes: rates shouldn’t keep rising, and the rules should be easier to predict. I don’t have a firm view on whether landlords or tenants should legally pay, or whether a tax on land value would be better.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: I wouldn’t put the bill on landlords. Small operators can struggle to understand the system and may quickly face enforcement if they miss a payment. Many want a shop, not to become experts in a complicated tax.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brash
turns.text: Should the Government do more about landlords who leave properties empty or charge high rents in places where local businesses are already struggling?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Empty properties should be brought back into use. In Altrincham, an independent food market helped draw people back after the Trafford Centre had pulled shoppers away. More independent businesses opened, and the council then helped make the town centre more welcoming.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: There’s a basic mismatch: people want properties to open or expand businesses, yet many units stand empty. Some owners don’t have the means or incentive to bring difficult buildings back into use.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Does improving a shop risk a higher rates bill, and how could that be fixed?

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Improvements to an existing property shouldn’t increase the value used to calculate its rates. Otherwise, businesses are discouraged from upgrading their premises.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Tax incentives could help businesses improve buildings. In Birkenhead, small grants helped owners make simple shopfront improvements. People in our Pride in Place area also say derelict buildings are a major reason they feel less proud of where they live.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Planning and licensing should work together. A business can wait months for planning permission, and objections can cause further delays, while it’s already paying rent.

turns.speaker: Lee Dillon
turns.text: If a business gets rates relief, how can we stop landlords simply raising the rent and taking that money?

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Rent reviews that can only go up are part of the problem. We should also make automatic rates relief available to more community-run organisations, not only registered charities.

chapters.title: Plans need local people and local capacity
chapters.takeaway: A national strategy can set direction, but towns need tailored plans, experienced local leaders and enough staff to put them into action.

turns.speaker: Alan Strickland
turns.text: High vacancy rates are still a serious problem in towns across the country. What needs to change so the Government’s high street strategy leads to visible improvements?

turns.speaker: Caireen Wackett
turns.text: There isn’t one solution for every town. The new strategy recognises that places have different needs, but councils still need help turning its ideas into action: they need tools, guidance, time and a way to measure social as well as financial benefits.

turns.speaker: Caireen Wackett
turns.text: Councils can be tempted to choose visible projects, like repaving a street, over smaller changes that may have a greater long-term effect. They need support to make those decisions.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: Some councils have received funding but don’t know where to start. They need the skills and capacity to understand their local area and decide what will work there.

turns.speaker: Helen Dickinson
turns.text: A national team or regional centres of expertise could help councils make plans and answer practical questions. Mayors could host those centres and support councils in their area.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Councils are under pressure from other duties and may lack the staff or experience for regeneration. In Wirral, a community-supported plan to rent out empty shops didn’t progress because the council couldn’t manage the extra work.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Regional authorities could offer expertise that an individual council doesn’t have, for example when a community wants to take over a long-derelict building. Local community leaders also need resources and some freedom to act.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brash
turns.text: Some towns have more shops and shopping areas than their local economy can sustain. How can an area make the difficult decision to change its offer, and who can help it do that?

turns.speaker: Caireen Wackett
turns.text: High streets now need to be places for services, learning and community life as well as shopping. Businesses may want to help, but councils need to bring many different organisations around the same table and agree a shared plan.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: Successful places are best understood by visiting them, not just by handing out a guide. Town leaders need the time and money to learn from places that have succeeded and adapt those lessons.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Plans have to suit the place. Events can bring visitors and spending: Parklife brought an estimated £13 million into the local economy, while Eurovision brought about £40 million to Liverpool.

turns.speaker: Liam Kelly
turns.text: We also need to trust local groups to take responsibility. Councils have to look after public money, but that can make it difficult for them to share power with community leaders.

chapters.title: Pubs, music and the night-time economy
chapters.takeaway: Night-time businesses provide jobs and community life, but witnesses said transport, safety and support for smaller venues are essential.

turns.speaker: Gagan Mohindra
turns.text: What helped improve Manchester’s night-time economy, and why did the Government offer a 20% rates discount to some venues?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Safety and transport were the priorities. People working late often couldn’t get affordable public transport home, and women and girls told us they sometimes had to walk.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Night buses, with fares capped at £2 across Greater Manchester, have made a real difference to workers. Pubs also matter as places where people can meet and avoid loneliness, not just as places to buy a drink.

turns.speaker: Gagan Mohindra
turns.text: Were you disappointed that nightclubs weren’t included in the rates discount?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: Yes. I thought 'clubs' included nightclubs, but it meant social clubs. I’ll keep pressing for nightclubs to be included. Small live music venues also need protection: many successful artists started in them.

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: It’s also harder for new bands to tour Europe after Brexit because they face visa costs at each border. We need to help smaller bands get started.

turns.speaker: Gagan Mohindra
turns.text: An association project to help 16-to-24-year-olds learn about electronic music was withdrawn after a funding shortfall. What happened?

turns.speaker: Sacha Lord
turns.text: The project planned courses with the Ministry of Sound and needed £100,000 but received £35,000. It was withdrawn and the association plans to apply again. I don’t handle its day-to-day operations, so I can’t explain the funding arrangements.

chapters.title: What should business rates become?
chapters.takeaway: The tax experts criticised the complexity of business rates, but differed on what should replace them and stressed that tax alone can’t revive high streets.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Would another discount for shops and hospitality make business rates even more complicated?

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: The bigger issue is that cutting rates mostly benefits landlords in the long run, because the tax is reflected in rents. So we’re spending public money on a policy that may not help the businesses it targets.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: The previous panel argued that landlords don’t always lower rents when a property is empty. Does that change your view?

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: It might, but I haven’t seen evidence that the rental market fails in this particular way. Landlords compete for tenants, so saying relief always benefits businesses needs to be backed up.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: I’d make the landlord responsible for paying, exempt improvements from the calculation, and reassess properties more often. The tenant’s overall costs shouldn’t change much, because rents would adjust over time.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Travers
turns.text: There are already so many discounts that councils need enormous spreadsheets to keep track of them. Even if landlords paid, there would still be political pressure for more exceptions.

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: The system should avoid punishing businesses for investing in their premises or growing. Because rates are based on property rather than profits, a business can face a higher bill even if it isn’t doing better.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Travers
turns.text: The Government has added different rates and discounts to protect some businesses, but each change creates more complexity. Property value also isn’t a reliable way to judge how profitable a business is.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: Special discounts create awkward boundaries. A shop may qualify if most of its business is selling vapes, for example, but a small change in how much it sells could suddenly change its tax bill.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Would a special rates rule be a good way to discourage vape shops?

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: No. If the aim is to tax vapes more, tax the vapes directly. Business rates tax a building, so they’re a roundabout and complicated way to do it.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Travers
turns.text: Business rates aren’t the main reason some high streets are struggling. Out-of-town shopping, more cars and online shopping have all changed how people shop, and tax discounts can’t reverse that.

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Tax reform should protect investment and consider how councils will replace stable rates income if taxes move towards profits, which can fall sharply in an economic downturn. High streets also need changes to planning and other local policies.

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Councils need the ability and resources to shape what their high streets become. Using business rates to target particular kinds of shop won’t solve that on its own.

chapters.title: Devolution and taxing online sales
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses disagreed on whether local areas should compete through tax cuts and whether online sales should face a new tax.

turns.speaker: Lee Dillon
turns.text: Councils can lose money when the rules for sharing business rates change. Could they have more certainty, and keep more of the money they raise to invest locally?

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Keeping more local revenue can help councils and mayors plan and borrow for future investment. But shifting local funding towards profits could make it less dependable when the economy slows.

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Travers
turns.text: The tax collected from businesses and the way central government shares money with councils are separate issues. A council can lose out under the funding system before a later change adjusts its share.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brash
turns.text: If mayors keep more local tax revenue, could struggling areas fall further behind places with stronger economies?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Travers
turns.text: The Government says areas should start off no better or worse, and that regions will keep some of the extra revenue if they grow. That gives them an incentive, but it also means places that grow more slowly may not be fully protected.

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: Regions with weaker tax income may also struggle to borrow for infrastructure. A national fund could help them invest even when their own revenues are low.

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: I’d be cautious about letting small regions cut taxes to attract businesses. It could create a race to offer lower taxes and a confusing patchwork of rules. Local areas might have more scope to target support at the businesses they need.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brash
turns.text: Could tax competition help attract investment to places like the North East, which has struggled to bring in private businesses?

turns.speaker: Professor Tony Travers
turns.text: It’s an argument worth considering, as places such as freeports and enterprise zones already use special tax arrangements. But tax competition between local areas can also have drawbacks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should the Government tax online sales to reflect how much shopping has moved online?

turns.speaker: Aditi Sriram
turns.text: We’ve proposed a 2% online sales tax because online businesses can sell a lot without occupying expensive high street space. It could charge only 1% on click and collect, exempt essentials, and avoid charging smaller businesses with sales below £500,000.

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: I don’t think there’s a tax problem to fix. The apparent advantage of online businesses is misleading if rates are ultimately reflected in rents. A new tax would need complicated rules about what counts as an online sale and could affect businesses across the economy.

turns.speaker: Chris Curtis
turns.text: Physical shops also give people a place to see and try products, and they bring life to town centres. Could a tax recognise those benefits?

turns.speaker: Dan Neidle
turns.text: Online shopping has real benefits too: it’s convenient and helps people who live far from shops or can’t easily leave home. We should be careful about using taxes to push people away from what they prefer.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today’s discussion shows that tax changes are only part of the answer. We also need local leadership, practical support for councils and community groups, and plans that fit each place and include independent businesses.
